h1: The 7 Best Soundbars With Subwoofers for Deeper TV Bass, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Soundbars With Subwoofers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 soundbars with subwoofers, from $25 to $500, compared on bass integration, wireless sub, EQ modes, virtual surround and value.
summary: The Polk Audio Signa S3 is the soundbar and subwoofer set to buy, with a wireless sub and a low-profile bar that slides under most TVs. The Hisense HS2100 adds six EQ modes and Bluetooth 5.3 for less, the Samsung HW-B550F brings DTS Virtual:X, and the Saiyin is the cheapest way to get a bundled sub.
intro: A soundbar with a subwoofer promises bass, but the promise is often broken by the way the pair is placed and connected. A wired subwoofer limits where it can sit, and a wireless one can still hum or drop if its pairing is poor. Before you compare watts or channel counts, ask how the sub connects to the bar and whether it can live in a corner or beside the sofa, where bass actually sounds best.

We reviewed seven bar-and-sub sets from $25 to $500, ranking them on subwoofer connection, EQ control, processing such as virtual surround, bar size and brand. Where a listing leaves out the power rating or the sub size, we have not guessed. Most of these are 2.1 designs, so expect widened stereo with bass, not true rear speakers.

products.name: Polk Audio Signa S3 Sound Bar & Wireless Subwoofer, Low-Profile Design
products.verdict: Polk's low-profile bar with a wireless subwoofer, built by an established speaker brand.
products.description:
The Signa S3 is a low-profile soundbar paired with a wireless subwoofer, from Polk Audio, a long-established speaker maker. It sits in the $200 to $500 range.

The S3 leads because Polk's background is loudspeakers, not accessories, and that tends to show in how well the bar and sub are voiced together. A wireless subwoofer means you can place the bass unit away from the TV stand, often beside a sofa where it fills the room better. The low-profile bar also slides under most televisions without blocking the screen or the remote sensor.

Buy it if you want dependable engineering and simple setup. The listing gives no power figure, so judge it on brand and design.
products.idealFor: Living rooms where clean design and dependable bass matter.

products.name: Hisense HS2100 2.1ch Soundbar with Wireless Subwoofer, Dolby Audio, DTS Virtual:X, 6 EQ Modes
products.verdict: Wireless sub, six EQ modes, Dolby Audio and DTS Virtual:X for $100 to $200.
products.description:
The HS2100 is a 2.1 channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer, Dolby Audio, DTS Virtual:X, six EQ modes and Bluetooth 5.3. Pricing falls between $100 and $200.

This set earns second place because it packs more adjustment than anything near its price. Six EQ modes let you favor dialogue for news, bass for movies or a flatter sound for music, and the Dolby and DTS processing widen the stage. Against the Polk it lacks a famous name and the listing does not stress build quality, but the savings are real.

Buy it for a bedroom or a mid-size living room where you want flexibility. Do not expect true rear speakers.
pros: Six EQ modes for different content
products.idealFor: Buyers who like to tune sound for different content.
products.skipIf: You want a heritage speaker brand.

products.name: Samsung B-Series Soundbar HW-B550F 2.1ch DTS Virtual:X with Subwoofer
products.verdict: DTS Virtual:X, bass boost and adaptive sound alongside a bundled subwoofer.
products.description:
Samsung's HW-B550F is a 2.1 channel bar with an included subwoofer, DTS Virtual:X, a bass boost mode and adaptive sound that adjusts to the content. It lands in the $200 to $500 range.

Third place is mostly about ecosystem and price. Adaptive sound adjusts the output for dialogue or action, which saves fiddling, and bass boost gives movies a push. It costs more than the Hisense and offers fewer manual EQ choices, so you are paying for the Samsung name and automatic processing rather than control.

Buy it if you already own a Samsung TV or prefer set-and-forget sound. If you like to tweak, take the Hisense.
products.idealFor: Samsung households that want hands-off sound.
products.skipIf: You want to fine-tune EQ yourself.

products.name: Polk Audio Signa S2 Ultra-Slim Sound Bar for Smart TV with Subwoofer
products.verdict: An ultra-slim Polk bar with an included subwoofer for tight TV stands.
products.description:
The Signa S2 is an ultra-slim soundbar for smart TVs with an included subwoofer, from Polk Audio. It sits in the $200 to $500 range and is the older sibling of the S3.

It ranks fourth because it offers the same brand pedigree in a thinner shape, which matters under TVs with low-slung feet. The listing does not describe the subwoofer as wireless the way the S3 does, so placement may be less flexible. It also comes from an earlier generation, so connectivity may feel dated next to the Hisense.

Buy it if your TV stand leaves no space for a taller bar. Otherwise the S3 is the better version of the same idea.
products.idealFor: TVs with short feet and little clearance.
products.skipIf: You want the newest connections or a wireless sub.

products.name: ULTIMEA 5.1 Sound Bar for Smart TV, Virtual Surround, Stereo Shelf System
products.verdict: A 5.1 virtual surround soundbar with a bundled subwoofer at a friendly price.
products.description:
The ULTIMEA is sold as a 5.1 soundbar for smart TVs with virtual surround and an included subwoofer, in the $100 to $200 range. The 5.1 label describes the processing and speaker count rather than a bar with true rear channels.

It takes fifth because virtual surround at this price is a real attraction, and a bundled sub adds bass. But the 5.1 figure should be read as a marketing claim: a single bar cannot place sound behind you the way separate rear speakers do. The brand has no speaker heritage.

Buy it if you want a wider sound on a modest budget. Keep expectations at 'bigger stereo', not true surround.
pros: Can serve as a shelf system
products.idealFor: Budget buyers who want a wider soundstage.

products.name: Assistrust Sound Bar with Subwoofer, 110W, Adjustable Deep Bass & Volume Boost, 3 Equalizer Modes
products.verdict: A 110W bar with a detachable design, adjustable bass and three EQ modes.
products.description:
The Assistrust soundbar lists 110W of power, a detachable design, adjustable deep bass and three equalizer modes, with a subwoofer included. It costs $50 to $100.

It lands sixth because it is the cheapest set with real tuning controls, and the detachable design lets you separate the bar into pieces for different placements. The 110W figure is a peak or system rating that companies use freely, so we do not treat it as proof of loudness. Without a named brand history, long-term reliability is unknown.

Buy it if you want adjustable bass and flexible placement on a small budget. Check the return policy.
cons: Power rating is a marketing figure
products.idealFor: Small budgets that want tuning controls.
products.skipIf: You want a trusted audio brand.

products.name: Saiyin Sound Bar with Subwoofer, Home Theater Surround System for TV PC
products.verdict: The cheapest bundled bar and sub, usable with both TVs and PCs.
products.description:
The Saiyin is a soundbar with a bundled subwoofer for TVs and PCs, sitting at $25 to $50. It is pitched as a home theater surround system, though the listing gives few technical details.

It finishes seventh because everything beyond the price is thin. There is no stated power, EQ or connection list, and the surround claim needs the usual skepticism. What it offers is the cheapest route to a bar-and-sub pair, and the PC compatibility is a handy bonus for a desk.

Buy it for a spare room, a dorm or a desktop where cost is the main constraint. Choose any of the six above for living-room use.
products.idealFor: Dorms, desks and spare rooms on the tightest budget.
products.skipIf: You want a main living-room system.

methodology.title: Subwoofer connection
methodology.description: We compared wireless and unspecified subwoofer links, since placement freedom decides how well the bass fills a room.

methodology.title: Brand and engineering
methodology.description: Established audio brands such as Polk and Samsung earned credit over unknown sellers, because voicing and reliability rarely show on a spec sheet.

methodology.title: Sound controls
methodology.description: EQ modes, bass adjustment and adaptive processing were weighed for how well they let you tune dialogue, movies and music.

methodology.title: Surround processing
methodology.description: Dolby Audio, DTS Virtual:X and virtual surround claims were treated as widening features, not as true rear channels.

methodology.title: Size and value
methodology.description: Low-profile and slim bars were rated for fit under TVs, and price tiers from $25 to $500 were set against the features delivered.

whatMatters.detail: A wireless subwoofer pairs with the bar over radio and needs only a power outlet, so it can sit anywhere. A wired one must stay near the bar. Check for the word wireless on the listing, and make sure there is an outlet near your preferred corner.

A 2.1 bar has left, right and subwoofer channels, and processing such as DTS Virtual:X simulates width. A bar labeled 5.1 without separate rear speakers uses the same trick. Expect a wider soundstage, not sound from behind you.

EQ modes let you favor voices, bass or balance, and a bass level control tames boom in apartments. Six modes give more room than three. Look for bass adjustment on the subwoofer or remote, which prevents late-night complaints.

A tall bar can block a TV's screen or remote sensor, while a low-profile or ultra-slim bar fits under it. Measure the gap between your stand and the TV. Also check whether the bar can be wall-mounted.

HDMI ARC or eARC is the easiest connection to a TV, optical is a common fallback and Bluetooth lets you stream music. Check your TV's ports against the bar's inputs. Bluetooth 5.3 on the Hisense offers a stable wireless link.

howToChoose.intro: Price sorts this group more than any other trait, so start with what you are willing to spend.

cards.label: Established brand
cards.text: Polk and Samsung bring voicing, support and a track record. The Polk Signa S3, Signa S2 and Samsung HW-B550F cost more but are better tuned and last longer.

cards.label: Budget brand
cards.text: ULTIMEA, Assistrust and Saiyin pack features into a small price. They suit spare rooms and desks, but support and long-term reliability are uncertain.

howToChoose.note: Choose an established brand for your main TV, and a budget brand only for secondary rooms.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A bass level control, a night mode and a wireless sub you can move away from shared walls. Lower volume at night while keeping dialogue clear.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Hisense HS2100 with six EQ modes and the Assistrust with adjustable bass give the most control. The Polk Signa S3 sounds balanced without tuning.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The soundbar is your main TV audio and you watch for hours. The Polk Signa S3 at $200 to $500 offers the cleanest bass and build.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The system is for a spare room, a desk or a dorm. The Saiyin or Assistrust deliver bass for $25 to $100.

faq.q: Will these soundbars work with any TV?
faq.a: Most connect by HDMI ARC, optical or Bluetooth, so they work with nearly any modern TV. Check which ports your TV has. Smart TVs generally support ARC.

faq.q: What is the common mistake buying a soundbar with a sub?
faq.a: Putting the subwoofer in the wrong place. Bass behaves differently by position, so move the sub around before settling. Corners boost bass, and the middle of a wall can sound thinner.

faq.q: Is a soundbar and sub worth it over TV speakers?
faq.a: Yes for most people. Built-in TV speakers are thin and can't produce bass. Even a budget set improves dialogue and movie impact.

faq.q: How do I pair a wireless subwoofer?
faq.a: Plug in both units and the sub usually pairs automatically. If not, press the pairing button on the sub until the light turns solid. Check the manual for the exact steps.

faq.q: How should I place the subwoofer?
faq.a: Start near the front, beside the TV stand, then try positions along a wall. Avoid enclosing it in a cabinet. Adjust bass level until voices stay clear.

faq.q: Can I use the budget bars with a PC?
faq.a: The Saiyin lists PC compatibility, and others may work through Bluetooth or an audio cable. Check the inputs before you buy. A desktop may need a 3.5 mm or USB connection.

finalTake: The Polk Audio Signa S3 is the soundbar and subwoofer set to buy if the TV is your main entertainment, thanks to its wireless sub and brand engineering. The Hisense HS2100 is the value pick with six EQ modes, and the Samsung HW-B550F suits set-and-forget households. Choose the ULTIMEA, Assistrust or Saiyin only for secondary spaces where price is the first rule.
